question: Two water-hating tails on one water-loving head make a _____ amphipathic, and that split alone is enough to send a sheet of them assembling into a membrane.
questions: Flippases and scramblases spend energy keeping each kind of _____ on the face of the membrane where it belongs, and a dying cell stops paying.
Some enveloped viruses carry a _____ normally hidden inside a living cell on their outer surface instead, so a scavenging cell swallows them as apoptotic debris.
abstract:
A phospholipid is two fatty acids joined to a polar head group, and in the glycerol phospholipids those chains are bound to a glycerol whose third carbon carries a phosphate instead. That phosphate usually has a small polar molecule attached to it, choline or ethanolamine or serine or inositol, and which one it carries is what names the lipid. Sphingomyelin is the exception, the only non-glycerol phospholipid in cell membranes, its two chains hanging from a head group built on serine rather than glycerol. All of them therefore have two hydrophobic tails and a hydrophilic head, which makes the molecule amphipathic, part water-soluble and part not, and that property is the basis on which biological membranes form. It is a strong enough property to work alone, since a synthetic compartment can be assembled out of a single lipid species with nothing else present.

The head group is not decoration, and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate is cut by phospholipase C into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, which in turn releases calcium inside the cell. The two faces of a membrane are not alike either, since phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin sit mostly in the outer leaflet while phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylinositol are enriched in the inner one. That arrangement is held rather than settled, maintained by ATP-driven flippases, floppases and scramblases that go on moving lipids across the bilayer. When a cell dies the arrangement collapses and phosphatidylserine appears on the outside, where it acts as an eat-me signal for scavenging cells, although on its own it is not enough to make one engulf. Several enveloped viruses exploit exactly that, carrying phosphatidylserine on their own membranes so that a cell takes them in as though they were the debris of a dead one.
